course_title: Masterclass- Advanced Research in the Humanities
course_description:
Students in this course engage in work-integrated learning, advanced humanities research methods and in-depth Indigenous research and Indigenous work ethics. The course takes a practical as well as a discussion-based approach, considering how humanities scholars engage with important contemporary issues, alongside key approaches and methods. HUMN3300 focuses on interdisciplinary thinking, Indigenous perspectives and practical skills in research and graduate career building and development.

This final course in the Advanced Humanities program is partly co-delivered with the UQ Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (ATSIS) Unit. It is designed to prepare you for life after graduation, and in our interactive two-hour lecture/workshops and seminars, we will negotiateﾠscholarly rigour and responsibility,ﾠcultural respectﾠand reconciliation and means of finding a rewarding career path. The first module of the course, 'Research Trajectories' focuses on research skills in the context of interdisciplinary humanities. We will discuss differences and similarities between different humanities disciplines,ﾠthe diverse cultural and social background of its academic community, the spaces,ﾠfacilities and methodologiesﾠit offers, and the communicative, digital and data-oriented techniques needed to navigate its range of pursuits of knowledge and experience. The second module, 'Work Trajectories', features career-focussed lectures and a five-weekﾠ'Public Humanities' mini-internship, where you will be given the opportunity to briefly try outﾠa humanities graduate work role (assigned in class). Finally, in the third and final module of the course, 'Cultural Trajectories', we will discuss how to find productive ways of working with, learning from and living alongside Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in our future cross-cultural society.

Throughout the course, we will share lectures with the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Unit course ABTS3020: Working with Indigenous People, where you will receive guidance, mentorship and inspiration from Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community leaders and scholars with prodigious experience of cross-community and cross-disciplinary collaboration. They will teach you where to start building relationships and how to maintain them.

course_aims: HUMN3300 aims to provide students with the skills needed to become mature scholars, andﾠenter the workforce asﾠproductive and respectful members of the community. You will learn to build a research project, consider all the ethical and practical aspects involved inﾠthe realisation of this project, and communicate and contribute respectfully with stakeholders. The course also includes a five-weekﾠindustry mini-internship arranged by the course coordinator, and a final module delivered by the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies Unit, focusing on ways you can use your research and skills ﾠto work towards reconciliation.ﾠ

learning_outcomes.description: Demonstrate an understanding of the basic principles of interdisciplinary research.

Be able to design relevant and feasible approaches to investigating research problems, including undertaking research at honours level, creating your own research questions, methodological approaches, and research designs.
Demonstrate knowledge of practical and theoretical issues underpinning work with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities.
Understand the types of discourses in which work with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people is situated - both historically and today - and your own positioning to these.
Use library and electronic resources at a level appropriate for your research and be able to locate appropriate materials for your area of study.
Communicate and interact competently and professionally in an industry environment (using a range of communication methods).
Demonstrate your skills and strengths in various career development situations.

assessment_details.task_description: Participation is essential for passing this course, and requires you to interact respectfully and learn from your peers. Students are expected to participate in tutorial discussions and complete tutorial tasks. This assessment requires you to show evidence of preparation for seminars and participate in large and small group discussions with relevant and well-focused comments. Participation in non-compulsory activities (like lectures and events organised through other students' internships) is not essential, but will earn you additional points. The participation component in this this course is slightly larger than other humanities courses, as it includes weekly pass/fail research or storying exercises in weeks 2-4 and 10-13, which should be completed by the end of the week AFTER their tutorials . assessment_details.title: Draft Research Questions
assessment_details.task_description: You should introduce 2-3 draft research questions in a BRIEF document (350 words in length, excluding bibliography), presenting a GENERAL area of study, a potential research approach, and an indicative bibliography (ca 3-5 sources) within the context of your preferred major. This is a research exercise, evaluating your skills, knowledge and approach in acquiring relevant research material - and it does not need to be related to your future honours plans (if you are planning to undertake honours). You will receive feedback on the level of sophistication of the formulation of your research questions in relation to your topic, sources and approach. learning_activities.topic: MID-SEMESTER BREAK

Week 1 Lecture: INTRODUCTION TO THE COURSE: The Future of Work, Humanities Research, and Cultural Collaboration LECTURE: Introduction to interdisciplinary research, the differences and similarities between humanities disciplines, and the future work place. PRE-RECORDED INTERVIEWS: Mixed UQ HASS Staff THERE ARE NO TUTORIALS THIS WEEK Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05, L07

Week 2 Lecture: RESEARCH TRAJECTORIES: Humanities Scholarship and Respectful Practice ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The first half of your lecture this week will be co-taught with the ATSIS unit, and you will hear Associate Professor Katelyn Barney speak about how you build a successful relationship with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities. METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: The second half of the lecture will focus on how you may start to formulate a humanities research project, emphasising the importance of honing in and refining a topic. We will also discuss the mini-internships that form part of this course. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05

Week 2 Tutorial WORKSHOP: We will discuss different types of scholarship, and different disciplinary methodologies and start working in discipline-specific groups to start workshopping your preferred research areas. We will discuss respectful ways of negotiating research relationships, including how to contact potential community mentors and supervisors, and how to negotiate a project with them. We will also workshop ways of formulating appropriate email conversations with people from different communities, and you will be encouraged to consider your choice of mini-internship for the course. PRACTICAL TASK: Supervisor/Mentor Email REQUIRED READINGS: Eco, Lewis and Bunda & Phillips (through Blackboard) Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Week 3 Lecture: RESEARCH TRAJECTORIES: Formulating the Right Questions ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The first half of your lecture this week will be co-taught with the ATSIS unit, and you will hear Quandamooka researcher and educator Dr Ren Perkins talk about how we can build more diversity into education in Queensland, and ways of making classrooms more welcoming to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: In the second half of the lecture, we will discuss how you go about communicating your research ideas clearly and efficiently when you first start formulating a project. We will consider how to spark the interest of a diverse audience by formulating the right research questions. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Week 3 Tutorial WORKSHOP: We will discuss research and work trajectories and consider the role our cultural, economic, religious, gender, and material background plays in the way we learn, and the opportunities available to us. We will also workshop ways of organising your research, and formulating ideas into a set of productive research questions. PRACTICAL TASK: Your Internship Choices & Rationale REQUIRED READING: Booth, Eco and Fredericks et. al., through Blackboard. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

Week 4 Lecture: RESEARCH TRAJECTORIES: Rethinking the Purpose of Research ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The first half of your lecture this week will be co-taught with the ATSIS unit, and you will hear Bidjara woman Professor Anne Pattel-Gray explore ideas of reciprocity, and the importance of developing strong relationships when working with Aboriginal people. She will also consider various aspects of ethics surrounding historical research. METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: In the second half of the lecture, we will discuss how humanities research and the tasks you've been doing throughout your degrees are in fact work skills. We will develop these practical skills to refine a research topic, find your original research contribution, alongside a discussion of how research skills may be used in a variety of future career paths. We will also discuss UQ Research Culture, Practice, and Resources and Ethics. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06

Week 4 Tutorial WORKSHOP: We will discuss 'ownership of history', ethical considerations in humanities research, practical work and research management skills, and the various ways in which humanities research may be translated into more mainstream humanities work. PRACTICAL EXERCISE: Career Trajectory Exercise REQUIRED READING: Watego, Booth, Eco, through Blackboard Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07

SHUT-UP-AND-WRITE SESSION This optional shut-up-and-write session running over Zoom on Thursday 20/6 at 9am-11am , will be offered as a means of sitting down together and get your first assessment for the course written in one go! It will be an opportunity to try out a traditional 'Pomodoro session'.

Week 5 Lecture: WORK TRAJECTORIES: How to Make the Most Out of your Work ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The first half of your lecture this week will be co-taught with the ATSIS unit, where Associate Professor Steve Salisbury will discuss how he has built and sustained relationships with Indigenous communities to aid his work in palaeontology (finding dinosaurs!). METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: In the second half of the lecture, we will discuss how to make the most out of your internship period. Learning outcomes: L04, L05, L06, L07
Week 5: NO TUTORIAL: Public Humanities Mini-Internship Students will devote this time to their mini-internships. Learning outcomes: L06, L07

Week 6 Lecture: CULTURAL TRAJECTORIES: Engagement and Project Lifecycles ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The first half of your lecture this week will be co-taught with the ATSIS unit, where Yimen and Goreng Gorgeng man Jim Walker will discuss key considerations underpinning work with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities. He will consider project lifecycle issues, including, project planning, relationship building and consultation, project implementation, participation, project reporting, dissemination and ongoing relationships. METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: In the second half of the lecture, we will discuss how to build your portfolio of work for submission at the end of your internship period. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07
Week 6: NO TUTORIAL: Public Humanities Mini-Internship Students will devote this time to their mini-internships. Learning outcomes: L06, L07

Week 7 Lecture: CULTURAL TRAJECTORIES: Creative Contexts ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The first half of your lecture this week will be co-taught with the ATSIS unit, where Dr Samantha Disbray will discuss her work in Indigenous language revitalisation. METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: In the second half of the lecture, we will discuss how to build your portfolio of work for submission at the end of your internship period. Learning outcomes: L02, L03, L04, L06, L07
Week 7: NO TUTORIAL: Public Humanities Mini-Internship Students will devote this time to their mini-internships. Learning outcomes: L06, L07

Week 8 Lecture: WORK TRAJECTORIES: Education & Academia In this lecture, you will get an introduction to what a career in education or academia may look like, with representatives discussing primary and secondary education from UQ's School of Education and representatives discussing academic work and tertiary education from UQ's School of Historical and Philosophical Inquiry and UQ's Centre for Western Civilisation. We will discuss the ways in which you could start such a journey - for example, the qualifications you need, and ways in which you can test if it suits you, and extra-curricular activities that may boost your CV. Invited Guests: TBA (teachers and academics) Learning outcomes: L06, L07
Week 8: NO TUTORIAL: Public Humanities Mini-Internship Students will devote this time to their mini-internships. Learning outcomes: L06, L07

Week 9 Lecture: WORK TRAJECTORIES: the GLAM Sector In this lecture, representatives from the UQ Art Museum, the UQ library and the Integrated Pathology Learning Centre will discuss what a career in museum, library and curatorial spaces may look like, and what you may need to do to get there. Invited Guests: TBA (curators, librarians and people working in government) Learning outcomes: L06, L07
Week 9: NO TUTORIAL: Public Humanities Mini-Internship Students will devote this time to their mini-internships. Learning outcomes: L06, L07

Week 10 Lecture: CULTURAL TRAJECTORIES: Working With Indigenous People PRE-RECORDED METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: All lecture material will be pre-recorded this week, due to the King's birthday public holiday. In the first half of the lecture, we will think through ideas, principles and theories of academic research and writing, specifically by looking in further detail at Tracey Bunda and Louise Phillips's 'storying' approach to research. Alongside Bunda & Phillip's work we will also discuss the key research ethics presented by Jim Walker - how to identify ethical questions and issues in your own research, how to manage these, and how to navigate them. We will consider the ways in which projects developed in collaboration with Indigenous people may take shape, and discuss key considerations underpinning work with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and communities. ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The second half of your lecture this week will be a recorded lecture from the ATSIS unit, where Professor Tracey Bunda will introduce you to 'storying' through her own deep ancestral connection to this concept, and the ethical mindset needed to conduct this work. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04, L05

Week 10 Tutorial WORKSHOP: In our tutorials we will discuss the difference between working 'with' and 'for' Indigenous people. We will also discuss 'Storying' as a methodology, and we will talk about ways in which we can use 'Storying' in our research and work lives. Alongside this week's lecture material, you'll need to revisit Jim Walker's week 6 lecture for this class. PRACTICAL EXERCISE: Positioning Exercise REQUIRED READING: Bunda & Phillips, Janke, Booth, through Blackboard Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L07

Week 11 Lecture: CULTURAL TRAJECTORIES: Engagement & Project Lifecycles METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: In the first half of the lecture, we will discuss how you build a project from an original idea, and how to find and sustain good relationships with collaborators, mentors and supervisors to support your work. It is about the importance of thinking expansively and between disciplines and communities! We will look at Steve Salisbury's work as an example of somebody who builds collaborations that stretch across many different layers of our community. RECORDED LECTURE SEGMENT: The second half of your lecture this week will be a recorded lecture segment by Professor Anna Johnston, from the School of Communication and Arts, who will tell you about one of her many research projects, and how she went about building this idea, step by step.

Week 11 Tutorial WORKSHOP: In our tutorials, we will explore ideas of reciprocity, and the importance of developing strong relationships when working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and when working collaboratively in general. Alongside the ideas presented in the week 11 lecture, you'll need to revisit Steve Salisbury's week 5 lecture for this class. PRACTICAL EXERCISE: AI Research Question Exercise REQUIRED READING: Bunda & Phillips, Wilson, Eco, ABC through Blackboard. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04

Week 12 Lecture: CULTURAL TRAJECTORIES: Locating Selves & Ethical Questions METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: In the first half of the lecture, we will consider language and naming processes. Why do names matter? Do we truly lose our identity if we lose our language and is there a way to recover them? If so, how do you go about recovering something that in some cases has been lost for generations? In this class, we'll revisit Samantha Disbray's lecture from week 7, alongside some new considerations from history and creative writing. We will continue Bunda & Phillips's discussions about 'storying', specifically considering the response-abilities it entails. We'll discuss what it means to write history, and taking ownership of a story. ATSIS LECTURE SEGMENT: The second half of your lecture this week will be a recorded lecture from the ATSIS unit, where the multi-award-winning Aboriginal author Professor Anita Heiss will discuss what goes into writing stories that are about your OWN history, and stories that matter to your people. She'll discuss why history and stories matter, and why they are always-already personal. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04

Week 12 Tutorial WORKSHOP: In our tutorials, we will discuss what it means to take ownership of a story, or an experience - and what it means to become part of the recovery of a story, an experience or a language. We will discuss this both from the point of view of Anita Heiss (as a writer and historian) and Samantha Disbray (who works in Indigenous language revitalisation). You will need to revisit the Samantha Disbray's lecture segment from week 7 for this class. PRACTICAL EXERCISE: Storying Exercise REQUIRED READING: Longbottom, Heiss, Disbray through Blackboard. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04, L05

Week 13 Lecture: CULTURAL TRAJECTORIES: Relationships & Relationality METHODS LECTURE SEGMENT: This final lecture of the course, will serve as a summary of the various trajectories explored. We will focus on the centrality of relationships and relationality - in professional life, research and our community as a whole. SECOND LECTURE SEGMENT: In the second half of the lecture, one of our previous Advanced Humanities students, Jocelyn Flynn, who is now Assistant Curator at the UQ Art Museum will join us to talk about how she has developed her cultural curatorial relationships. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04, L05

Week 13 Tutorial WORKSHOP: In our final tutorials, Jocelyn Flynn will join us and lead an exercise where you will be encouraged to explore your relationships and consider what it means to be a good ally, mentor and mentee. We will discuss what we have learnt in the course, and we will will consider avenues for future growth. PRACTICAL EXERCISE: Welcome to Country REQUIRED READING: How to Give a Good Welcome to Country (UQ) Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04, L05
INDIVIDUAL INTERVIEWS You will be given a time slot for a 15-minute graduate mock-job interview. Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04, L05, L06, L07

SHUT-UP-AND-WRITE SESSION This optional shut-up-and-write session running over Zoom on Monday 2/11 at 9am-11am , will be another opportunity to try out a traditional 'Pomodoro session'. For those of you who are doing honours, this could be an opportunity to start drafting your honours proposals. Alternatively, you can use this time to work on one of your assessments from another course.
